system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-08-15 19:02:00 to 2186-08-25 16:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of dilated non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on warfarin, prior strokes, type II diabetes, and morbid obesity was admitted for acute on chronic systolic heart failure exacerbation presenting with worsening shortness of breath, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema. The exacerbation was attributed to high dietary salt intake and intermittent noncompliance with diuretic therapy. He was treated with 160 mg of IV furosemide over two days, resulting in clinical improvement with reduced edema and weight loss from 139 kg to 128.7 kg. His heart function remained stable with an ejection fraction of 30%, and no acute ischemia was noted. Chronic issues including bilateral foot ulcers, blepharitis, and obstructive sleep apnea were monitored, with no signs of infection in the wounds. He was discharged home on his prior medications, including torsemide 60 mg twice daily, with instructions for strict low-salt diet, daily weight monitoring, and follow-up for cardiac MRI, podiatry, and ophthalmology.

Right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health
Aftercare following surgery of the musculoskeletal system, NEC
Diabetes with ophthalmic manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ yo M with PMH notable for atrial 
fibrillation/atrial flutter (CHADS2 of 5) on coumadin, dilated 
cardiomyopathy with recent exacerbation of systolic CHF ___ 
on echo from ___, DM, HLD, and hx. of previous multiple CVAs 
who is admitted for a GI bleed and found to have colonic mass on 
colonoscopy with no evidence of metastases on CT scan. Patient 
was initially admitted to the ICU for concern of rapid bleeding 
from lower source. He was supported with IVF and when his Hct 
remained stable, he was transferred to the floor. Colonoscopy 
and EGD were performed and he was found to have a colonic mass 
in the descending colon concerning for malignancy; superficial 
biopsy revealed high grade dysplasia. There were also scattered 
polyps throughout the colon but these were not removed due to 
concern for bleeding in the context of patient's elevated INR. 
CT scan did not show definitive evidence of mestastasis. After 
discussion of risks and benefits, the patient elected to undergo 
surgical resection of the mass during this admission. 

As such, he was medically optimized for surgery with the help of 
cardiology in the following ways: his warfarin was stopped on 
admission and when his INR was less than 2 he was started on a 
heparin drip, which was stopped 4 hours prior to surgery. For 
his CHF, his torsemide, ramipril metalazone were all held on 
admission due to concern for bleeding. His diuretics were 
restarted the day before surgery and then held the day of 
surgery. His metoprolol was fractionated to tartrate and 
continued the day of surgery. His ramipril was held throughout 
admission due to low systolic blood pressures. 

Patient was taken to the operating room on ___ where he 
underwent a laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy. The procedure was 
uncomplicated; please see operative report for further details. 
The patient was admitted to the Colorectal Surgery service for 
standard post-op care. 

Per pathway, patient's diet was advanced starting POD1 from 
clears and was tolerating a regular diet on POD2. He received 
Dilaudid PCA for pain control initially and transitioned to oral 
analgesics once tolerating oral intake. Patient's systolics 
ranged from ___ to low 100s. He did have a couple of episodes of 
hypotension with systolics to the ___ that responded with 
albumin boluses. He also had very brief, asymptomatic, and 
self-resolving runs of V-tach. 

Anticoagulation was resumed on POD2 with his home dose of 
Coumadin and heparin gtt bridge. He reached therapeutic on his 
INR on POD4. Per Cardiology, his home metoprolol and torsemide 
were restarted on POD2, ramipril on POD3, and spironolactone on 
POD4. Patient was instructed to restart metolazone on POD5 (day 
after discharge). His cardiac status remained stable throughout 
the hospital course.

Patient was medically ready for discharge on POD4. At time of 
discharge, he was tolerating a regular diet, voiding freely, 
passing flatus and stool, and ambulating independently. Labs on 
day of discharge did show hypokalemia and he was repleted.  
Patient was offered ___ services but declined. He was discharged 
home in good condition.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

You were admitted to ___ for a GI bleed and found to have a 
mass in your colon concerning for cancer. There were other 
polyps seen in your colon as well for which you will need to 
undergo another colonoscopy with Dr. ___ in ___. 
You have done well and are now ready for discharge home. 
Multiple follow up appointments were made for you to see your 
healthcare providers, and it is important for you to keep these. 
You also need labs (INR, electrolytes) drawn on ___ 
___ and have the results faxed to Dr. ___ Dr. 
___. 

In regards to your COLON SURGERY, samples from your colon were 
taken and this tissue has been sent to the pathology department 
for analysis. You will receive these pathology results at your 
follow-up appointment. If there is an urgent need for the 
surgeon to contact you regarding these results they will contact 
you before this time. You have tolerated a regular diet, are 
passing gas and your pain is controlled with pain medications by 
mouth. You may return home to finish your recovery.

Please monitor your bowel function closely. You may or may not 
have had a bowel movement prior to your discharge which is 
acceptable, however it is important that you have a bowel 
movement in the next ___ days. After anesthesia it is not 
uncommon for patients to have some decrease in bowel function 
but you should not have prolonged constipation. Some loose stool 
and passing of small amounts of dark, old appearing blood are 
expected. However, if you notice that you are passing bright red 
blood with bowel movements or having loose stool without 
improvement please call the office or go to the emergency room 
if the symptoms are severe. If you are taking narcotic pain 
medications there is a risk that you will have some 
constipation. Please take an over the counter stool softener 
such as Colace, and if the symptoms do not improve call the 
office. If you have any of the following symptoms please call 
the office for advice or go to the emergency room if severe: 
increasing abdominal distension, increasing abdominal pain, 
nausea, vomiting, inability to tolerate food or liquids, 
prolonged loose stool, or extended constipation.

You have ___ laparoscopic surgical incisions on your abdomen 
which are closed with internal sutures and a skin glue called 
Dermabond. These are healing well however it is important that 
you monitor these areas for signs and symptoms of infection 
including: increasing redness of the incision lines, 
white/green/yellow/malodorous drainage, increased pain at the 
incision, increased warmth of the skin at the incision, or 
swelling of the area. Please call the office if you develop any 
of these symptoms or a fever. You may go to the emergency room 
if your symptoms are severe.

You may shower; pat the incisions dry with a towel, do not rub. 
The small incisions may be left open to the air. If closed with 
steri-strips (little white adhesive strips) instead of 
Dermabond, these will fall off over time, please do not remove 
them. Please no baths or swimming for 6 weeks after surgery 
unless told otherwise by your surgical team.

You will be prescribed a small amount of the pain medication 
oxycodone. Please take this medication exactly as prescribed. 
You may take Tylenol as recommended for pain. Please do not take 
more than 3000mg of Tylenol daily. Do not drink alcohol while 
taking narcotic pain medication or Tylenol. Please do not drive 
a car while taking narcotic pain medication.

No heavy lifting greater than 6 lbs for until your first 
post-operative visit after surgery. Please no strenuous activity 
until this time unless instructed otherwise by Dr. ___.

In regards to your HEART FAILURE, weigh yourself every morning, 
call your PCP if weight goes up more than 3 lbs. Please also 
take your cardiac medications.

In regards to your ATRIAL FIBRILLATION, please continue to take 
Coumadin at your usual dose. You need your INR checked on 
___ please let your ___ know of these results 
so your dosage can be adjusted accordingly.

Thank you for allowing us to participate in your care! Our hope 
is that you will have a quick return to your life and usual 
activities. Good luck!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in because of some blood when you went to the bathroom?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a small spot on the toilet paper. Bright red. I was at my PCP’s office and they sent me here right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’re keeping you in the ICU tonight just to be safe in case there’s more bleeding. Your blood count is stable so far, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling okay. A little lightheaded earlier, but not now. I’ve lost about 25 pounds since my last hospital stay with the heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see your diuretics were increased recently. That explains the weight loss. We’ve paused your torsemide and metolazone for now because of the bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Should I be worried about my heart swelling back up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Your lungs are clear and your oxygen is good. We’ll restart the diuretics once we’re sure the bleeding is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Coumadin? I’m on that for my atrial fibrillation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped your Coumadin for now. Your INR was 1.9, which is a bit high for procedures. We’ll start a heparin drip once your INR drops below 2 to keep your clot risk low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning, you’ll have an EGD and colonoscopy to find where the blood is coming from. We’ll keep you NPO after midnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your foot X-ray showed some changes near the second toe — possible infection or osteomyelitis. The podiatry team will see you later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I thought the amputation healed. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we need to monitor. Your foot culture grew staph, but it’s sensitive to antibiotics. We’ll likely start something once we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Any news on the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You’re still scheduled for the scopes today. We’ll know more after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___ , I have results from your colonoscopy. There’s a mass in your sigmoid colon. The biopsy showed high-grade dysplasia — that means it’s very likely cancerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cancer? Oh no. Is it spread?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan didn’t show any metastases. That’s good news. But we do see enlarged lymph nodes nearby, so we’ll remove some during surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I was just in the hospital for my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But given your heart history, we’ve consulted cardiology. They agree surgery is safe if we manage your anticoagulation and heart meds carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy — removing the part of the colon with the tumor. It’s minimally invasive and recovery is usually quicker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? My blood pressure was low earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your ramipril because of the low BP. Your metoprolol has been switched to the IV form so we can control it better during surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. When would this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for Thursday — day after tomorrow. That gives us time to optimize your labs and get you ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your INR is now 1.8. We’ll stop the heparin tonight and resume it after surgery as a bridge back to Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diuretics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted torsemide yesterday. You’ll stop it again the morning of surgery. Same with metolazone — you’ll restart it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___ . You’re back from surgery. The laparoscopic colectomy went well. They removed the tumor and nearby lymph nodes. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How do I feel? I’m a bit groggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You had a brief episode of V-tach, but it resolved on its own. Your heart rhythm is now irregular due to your AFib, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a drop last night, but it responded to albumin. We’re watching it closely. You’re on a clear liquid diet now and will advance as you tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your incisions are healing well. We’ve started your Coumadin again today, along with heparin, to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back on blood thinners already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of your atrial fibrillation. We’ll monitor your INR daily. It’s 2.0 this morning — on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Metoprolol and torsemide are back on. Ramipril will restart tomorrow. Spironolactone will start on day four.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You passed gas and had a small bowel movement — great signs your gut is waking up. We’re switching you to a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry. Can I have real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start with soft foods. And you’re walking to the bathroom on your own — that’s excellent for recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.2 — therapeutic. We’ll stop the heparin. Your kidney function is improving too — creatinine down to 1.1.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my potassium? I remember it was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 3.2 this morning. We gave you supplements. You’ll need to keep an eye on it at home with your diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. So am I going home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all goes well. You’re tolerating food, passing stool, and your pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your incisions look great — no redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your Coumadin daily. Check your INR in a few days. Watch for fever, redness, or bleeding from the incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Restart metolazone tomorrow. Weigh yourself daily. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the foot infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The team will follow up with podiatry. Keep the wound clean and watch for swelling or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the colon results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pathology report will come in a few days. You’ll discuss it at your follow-up with the surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have to go back for another colonoscopy too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in six months, to check the other polyps. It’s important for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Take it easy for a few weeks — no heavy lifting. And call us if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gently. Pat the incisions dry. No baths or swimming for six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a small prescription for oxycodone. Use only as needed. Tylenol is fine too — just don’t exceed 3,000 mg a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No driving, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct — not while on narcotics. And no alcohol with those meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve got this. We’ll fax your discharge summary to your PCP and specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I feel lucky to be here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — if you pass bright red blood or have severe belly pain, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m not taking any chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. Really.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Goodbye for now.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation on Coumadin, dilated cardiomyopathy, systolic heart failure, diabetes, and morbid obesity was admitted for evaluation of bright red blood per rectum. He had recently lost 25 pounds due to increased diuretic therapy for heart failure. Initial workup revealed stable hemoglobin but a concerning colonic mass in the sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy and EGD showed high-grade dysplasia in the mass and gastritis, while CT scans showed no metastases. After multidisciplinary coordination and cardiac optimization, he underwent a laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy with lymph node excision. Postoperatively, he had brief episodes of hypotension and asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia, both managed conservatively. His anticoagulation was bridged with heparin, and cardiac medications were carefully resumed. He developed transient hypokalemia, which was corrected. He recovered well, tolerating a regular diet, ambulating independently, and passing stool. He was discharged home on postoperative day four with instructions to restart metolazone, monitor weight and INR, and follow up for pathology results and repeat colonoscopy in six months.
